A wall of vines appears out of the morning fog across the Mosel River in Germany. The famously steep slate slopes of the Mosel produce some of the world’s most riveting wines and are among the most notorious to work. The combination of incline and slippery shards of loose slate makes the vineyards both difficult and dangerous. But the Riesling is worth it.

title: Hip-Hop Doesn’t Need Wine, But Wine Just Might Need Hip-Hop
summary:

The post Hip-Hop Doesn’t Need Wine, But Wine Just Might Need Hip-Hop appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Despite the fading evening light on Lankershim Boulevard, I had to squint a bit in the dim light of the club. The wide-open floor was already beginning to fill up with fashionably dressed people as the sounds of hip-hop coursed through the club’s speakers at a relatively subdued volume.

A glance around the room suggested the action was on the periphery, where several individuals stood behind small tables each holding a couple of wine bottles. I grabbed a proffered wine glass from a side table (noting with a somewhat delayed shock that it was a Zalto Universal) and headed for my first taste, walking up to a table staffed by a young woman wearing a hoodie. With a pleasant hello and a smile, Saskia de Rothschild poured me a taste of 1985 Lafite, and that is when I knew I was in for a wine event unlike anything else I had ever experienced.

This was Vin et Hip-Hop Los Angeles, the first US version of a wine event originally held in 2022 at the venerable Château du Clos de Vougeot in Burgundy. The event sprang from a collaboration between vintner Jeremy Seysses of Domaine Dujac, podcaster and educator Jermaine “Wolf of Wine” Stone, and Milena Berman and Loïc Lamy, the duo behind the experiential marketing agency Hautes Côtes. In its first incarnations, it brought hip-hop performers to the heart of Burgundy for a music-festival-meets-wine-tasting event celebrating two expressions of craft that have historically had only the most tenuous of relationships.

The Birth of Vin et Hip-Hop

As a recent Art History graduate working in Los Angeles art galleries, the young California-born Milena Berman jumped at the chance when she received an offer to join an art tourism company based in Burgundy.

“Three weeks later, sight unseen, I moved to Beaune,” she said when I interviewed her in March. It was something of a dream job, creating bespoke tours to art fairs and museums all over Europe for high-level donors to top museums around the world. But like so many things during the Pandemic, it all came crashing to a halt. Berman looked around at her options and decided she might be able to work in wine.

“I reached out to Domaine Dujac, and I said, I’m not sure what I can do at a winery, maybe marketing and sales,” she recalled. “And they were like, ‘Yeah, we don’t do marketing and sales.'”

But the family clearly saw something in the young woman and found her a position on the administrative side of the business, working closely with winemaker Jeremy Seysses, particularly on activities supporting The Roots Fund, something meaningful to her as an American in the midst of the #BlackLivesMatter movement and moment.

As the world opened back up, Berman decided to leave Dujac and launch her own agency, Hautes Côtes, with partner Loïc Lamy, but just before she did, she ended up helping Dujac put on an event that featured podcaster Jermaine Stone. Berman and Stone hit it off and began discussing other potential events they could collaborate on, and they settled on the idea of a post-harvest party.

“I said to Jermaine that I’d make grilled cheese sandwiches and we could find a DJ, and he could do the playlist for the event, and I could ask Jeremy [Seysses] and a few other winemakers to pour a white wine, and so we made a terrible little logo, and made an announcement, and it sold out in minutes,” said Berman. “We were like, ‘Who’s coming to this?'”

Young interns from all over the world staying in Burgundy for their harvest jobs snapped up many of the inexpensive tickets, but some were locals, like Dominique Lafon.

“Dominique said, ‘This is amazing, next year you have to do it at Clos de Vougeot,’ and we were like, ‘Yeah, right,’ and he said, ‘No, I’m serious, I will go with you and tell them they should do this,'” recalls Berman.

Come as You Are

With Lafon’s urging, the Château du Clos de Vougeot agreed, and Vin et Hip Hop was born. When word came through the grapevine that Mike D was coming to Burgundy to be inducted into the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin, the opportunity proved too good to pass up. Introductions were made, and the Beastie Boys founder agreed to DJ the inaugural event following his induction.

From the outset, the organizers envisioned an experience with far more accessibility than the black-tie affairs that have made the Château du Clos de Vougeot legendary among wine lovers.

“We were like, ‘Come in your jeans, come as you are,'” said Berman, “and we wanted the tickets to be less than 100 bucks with dinner included.” The organizers set aside a portion of the proceeds to benefit The Roots Fund.

The resulting event was certainly unlike anything that the Château had ever hosted: 700 young people (and a few older folks, too) partying to the sounds of hip-hop while tasting Burgundies from top producers. In a model that has continued through all subsequent events, producers made bottles available for sale to attendees, who, in the fashion of La Paulée, could open them and share with friends, acquaintances, and strangers throughout the night.

“We talk about how wine can reach different audiences, but sometimes wine needs help,” said Icy Liu, of Becky Wasserman & Co., one of the event’s sponsors. “Wine has had a very different way of relating and representing itself and being engaged with culture in a certain way for a long time, but it’s maybe a bit out of touch with the mainstream of the culture. Hip-hop is cool. The artists are always driving the dialogue with what we’re wearing, where we’re eating, and what we’re doing. Hip-hop is shaping cultural identity.”

That sense of connection with mainstream culture, as well as the passionate communities that have arisen around hip-hop, became a core tenet of the event, which now describes one of its primary goals as “bridging worlds through cultural exchange.”

In addition to the several editions of the event held at Clos de Vougeot, the organizers have also put on Pop et Hip-Hop in the Champagne region. After several years of European events, American wine and hip-hop lovers clamored for a domestic version, and in a lobbying campaign that I imagine was something like the competition for Olympic host cities, Los Angeles won the right to host the first event on American soil.

A Los Angeles Exclusive

The 2026 event in Los Angeles at Verse was unlike any wine event I’ve attended across a number of dimensions. The wines being poured for attendees were spectacular: Vintage Krug Champagne, Billecart-Salmon Elisabeth Salmon Rosé, Domaine de Montille 1er Cru Les Sizies, Dalla Valle Maya, Harlan Estate, Colgin IX Estate, Jaboulet Hermitage La Chapelle, Château Lafleur, Comtes Lafon 1er Cru Meursault-Charmes, Domaine Dujac 1er Cru Aux Combottes, Michel Lafarge Volnay, Domaine Fourrier 1er Cru Combe aux Moines Gevrey-Chambertin, and yes, 1985 Château Lafite Rothschild, among many others.

The crowd was impressively diverse, in both age and race, and the vibe was electric even before the performers took the stage. Common, Keyon Harrold, Dominique Sanders, Jason L. Martin, Dilated Peoples, and a guest appearance from Wiz Khalifa kept the room thumping until late, while the parking lot was filled with food trucks dishing up everything from smash burgers to caviar bumps.

A team of sommeliers behind the bar handled an enthusiastic crowd of spendy wine lovers who were more than happy to deplete the stocks of wines from Burgundy, Champagne, Napa, Bordeaux, Abruzzo, and the Rhône being sold at eye-poppingly excellent prices. Not to unnecessarily tantalize you, but a 2021 Arnoux-Lachaux Vosne-Romanée was on offer that night for $250. Try to find that bottle at retail today, and you’ll pay somewhere north of $600.

The catch to all this was the price of entry. This party and concert (which Hautes Côtes flew me down to LA to attend) had no tickets. Attendance was by invitation only. And to secure an invitation, you had to purchase a seat at one of the many winemaker dinners that preceded the event, with price tags starting at $850 and going up to more than $2,500. I believe the capacity of the club topped out at around 200 people.

Standing there with a $78 hand-blown wine glass filled with $500-per-bottle Burgundy, watching Common freestyle his way through a verse about drinking wine, I didn’t exactly feel part of anything close to “the mainstream.” I was lucky enough to attend an event the likes of which few people have ever had the opportunity to experience. Rarified doesn’t begin to describe it, and that struck me as quite the opposite of what Vin et Hip Hop was trying to achieve, significant donations to The Roots Fund notwithstanding.

When I put this to winemaker Jeremy Seysses and to Berman, they both agreed that the level of exclusivity featured in this event was not in alignment with the mission and vision for Vin et Hip-Hop long term, and reflected more of the specific opportunity they had to partner with the Verse supper club, owned by Grammy-award-winning sound engineer Manny Marroquin.

“I want to see something much bigger in the US,” said Seysses, “closer to or even bigger than what we do at Clos de Vougeot, with similar ticket prices.”

I’d love to see that, too.

A Deserving Synergy

At a time when wine seems to be struggling for relevance with younger generations of drinkers, and demand is shrinking, the appeal of Vin et Hip-Hop becomes obvious. Making inroads with hip-hop’s own diverse audience, and more specifically Black wine drinkers, seems not just smart but imperative. Taking wine off its pedestal and putting it in contexts where it connects with other dimensions of culture offers an opportunity to have different conversations or even just experience wine in different moods. A festival called Blood of Gods, named after a ‘zine of the same name, is doing something similar with heavy metal music in Washington State.

Can events such as these truly change the world of wine, a few hundred people at a time? That remains to be seen. At the very least, they represent something novel and exciting in an industry that seems convinced we’ll all be enthused by a press release touting the latest 90-point scores or the achievement of a new sustainability certification.

Wine needs to be more fun. And it needs to be more fun to a lot more people than it has in the past if the industry is going to survive and thrive. It also needs to connect with communities of passion, and especially those that have at their center things other than wine itself.

Wine also needs to be a bigger, more welcoming place for populations that have historically not been part of the wine conversation, for people who haven’t historically seen many people who look like them engaging with and enjoying wine.

These, I believe, are the glimmers of promise that can be seen amidst the strobes and heard amongst the thumping bass beats of Vin et Hip-Hop. Whether Vin et Hip-Hop can hold onto that promise while retaining its founding ethos (come in your jeans, come as you are) is the harder trick, and the one worth watching (or listening) for.

The next Vin et Hip-Hop event will take place on October 14th, 2026 at the Château du Clos de Vougeot in Burgundy. Tickets went on sale today, September 16th at 5 PM Central European Time, and were sold out almost instantly, as 5300 people attempted to register simultaneously.

The Hatues Côtes team is already working on Vin et Hip Hop for 2027, with events planned in New York and Los Angeles in March, Champagne in June, and another Burgundy event in October. Bordeaux is purportedly in the works too.

title: Vinography Unboxed: Week of 9/6/26
summary:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking

The post Vinography Unboxed: Week of 9/6/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This week I received a couple of wines from Shared Notes Wines, the Sauvignon Blanc-focused project by the wife-and-husband winemaking team of Bibiana Gonzalez Rave and Jeff Pisoni. I’m reviewing both of the wines they make under that brand this week, and both are excellent, with the caveat that their packaging in big, heavy bottles is effectively a big middle finger to the environment. There’s just no reason to package wines like this in bottles that literally weigh more than the wine they contain. Jeff and Bibiana should know better. OK, off of my soapbox, I think I prefer the straight Sauvignon Blanc to their blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon, at least in the 2025 vintage. I love that both are harvested to result in lean, snappy wines that still have some herbaceous qualities in addition to their sunny fruit. Not everyone will be on board with paying nearly $100 for a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, but those who are will find these wines enjoyable.

Chateau Montelena sent through their Sauvignon Blanc as well, and it seemed rather subdued in comparison to the Shared Notes wines, though it is also half the price.

This week I’m reviewing the Cuvée Esme Ann Chenin Blanc from Las Jaras Wines, which is one of my favorite California Chenins for its reductive, snappy, mouthwatering qualities. The fruit comes from the Junius Vineyard (formerly known as Norgard) in Mendocino County and is barrel-fermented and aged in oak, followed by 9 months in stainless steel.

This week I’m also reviewing another batch of wines from Geographic Wines, a project based in Portugal focused on making wines from many of the country’s different wine regions. This week I enjoyed their white blend from old vines in the Douro as well as their old vine red blend of more than 45 grape varieties from the same place. Sadly, these wines aren’t well distributed outside of Europe, so no buying links to offer to my readers for these. Also, the brand’s website is broken, so I can’t even give you somewhere to learn more about them.

I’ve got a couple of old-vine Zinfandels to recommend this week, from Limerick Lane Cellars, whose Marquis Zinfandel comes from a number of storied old-vine Zinfandel vineyards around Sonoma County and has a tremendous juicy lift with little trace of its substantial alcohol levels.

The 2023 Ridge Lytton Springs is a perennial favorite of mine for its complexity, impressive ageworthiness, and just generally mouthwatering offering of blue and black fruits. The 2023 vintage is an impressive edition of this wine that will likely be great for decades.

Speaking of the 2023 vintage, it also did good things for Tierra Roja wines in Napa’s Oakville AVA, where proprietor Linda Neal farms just over 4 acres of Cabernet Sauvignon. Neal worked as a vineyard manager for others in Napa for many years before deciding to focus exclusively on her own property. She makes just a single wine from the plot each year, and the 2023 vintage is certainly one of the best that winemaker Benoit Touquette has made for her.

The name Giacomo Borgogno is well known in Italy’s Piedmont region for having made Barolo since 1761, making it the oldest continuously operating producer in the region. As in many European countries, Italian wines are subject to tasting panels before they are approved to carry the Barolo DOCG designation. In 2005, Borgogno submitted two cask samples to the tasting commission, and one was rejected for not seeming typical in color, despite being made exactly the same as the one that had been accepted. In protest, Borgogno declassified the wine, and No Name Langhe Nebbiolo was born, bearing the designation “a protest label” against appellation bureaucracy. Since then, the Borgogno family has continued to deliberately declassify a portion of their Barolo production each year to make the wine. It is always excellent.

Notes on all these below.

Tasting Notes

2025 Shared Notes “Les Leçons des Maîtres” White Blend, Russian River Valley, Sonoma, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass—nearly colorless—this wine smells of passionfruit, green bell peppers, and honeysuckle. In the mouth, silky, salty flavors of chopped green herbs, green apple skin, and gooseberries have a nice brightness thanks to excellent acidity. A blend of 75% Sauvignon Blanc and 25% Semillon. 13.5% alcohol. 266 cases made. Comes in an unnecessarily heavy bottle weighing 1.54 kg when full. Score: around 9. Cost: $95. click to buy.

2025 Shared Notes “Les Pierres Qui Décident” Sauvignon Blanc, North Coast, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of green apple, passionfruit, cut grass, and a hint of green bell peppers. In the mouth, candied green apple, passionfruit, and gooseberry flavors are electrically bright with excellent acidity and shot through with a hint of crushed nuts and alfalfa. Bright and juicy. A blend of fruit from Sonoma County (70%) and Napa County (30%). 12.87% alcohol. Comes in a nasty, heavy bottle weighing 1.63 kg when full. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $95. click to buy.

2025 Chateau Montelena Sauvignon Blanc, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Palest greenish gold in color, this wine smells of lime zest, green apples, and white flowers. In the mouth, green apple and kiwi notes have a faint grassy quality to them, as well as decent acidity. 14.2% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2023 Las Jaras “Cuvée Esme Anne” Chenin Blanc, Mendocino County, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of struck match, Asian pear, honeysuckle, and candied ginger. In the mouth, candied ginger, Asian pear, struck match, and wet pavement flavors are saline and bright with juicy acidity. Lean and bright, with lovely persistence. Barrel-fermented and aged in oak, followed by 9 months in stainless steel. Bottled unfiltered. 13% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $68.

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Vinhas Velhas Chão de Areia” Vinho Branco, Douro, Portugal
Pale yellow-gold in color, this wine smells of yellow plum, nectarine, and struck flint. In the mouth, salty flavors of unripe nectarines, pomelo zest, saffron, and dried herbs are bright and juicy with a hint of oaky nuttiness. Excellent acidity. A field blend of Rabigato, Viosinho, Gouveio, Códega de Larinho, Síria, and Folgasão. 12% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: ??

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Canais” Touriga Nacional, Douro, Portugal
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black tea, black cherries, crushed peppercorns, and dried herbs. In the mouth, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of black cherries, black tea, and dried herbs. Very good acidity. The tannins gain weight and stiffness with time. 12.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $??

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Vinhas Velhas Almendra” Red Blend, Douro, Portugal
Medium to dark garnet in color, this wine smells of black cherries, black plum, bergamot, earth, and dried flowers. In the mouth, smooth, suede-like tannins coat the mouth and surround a core of black cherries, black plum, currants, dried herbs, and wildflowers. Excellent acidity, lovely balance, and poise. Comes from a field blend of more than 45 different varieties planted in 1850. 12.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $??

2023 Ridge Vineyards “Lytton Springs” Red Blend, Dry Creek Valley, Sonoma, California
Dark purple in the glass, this wine smells of blackberries, black pepper, boysenberries, and cocoa powder. In the mouth, blackberry pie and cocoa powder flavors are wrapped in powdery, mouth-coating tannins that linger with licorice, dried herbs, and sandalwood in the finish. Excellent acidity and balance. 14.4% alcohol. A blend of 76% Zinfandel, 14% Petite Sirah, 7% Carignan, 2% Alicante Bouschet, and 1% Mataro. Vineyard planted in 1905. 11,800 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $56. click to buy.

2023 Limerick Lane Cellars “Marquis” Zinfandel, Russian River Valley, Sonoma, California
Very dark garnet in color, this wine smells of blackberries, licorice, and flowers. In the mouth, juicy floral flavors of boysenberries, raspberries, and orange peel are wrapped in supple, athletic tannins. Great acidity. 15.1% alcohol. 350 cases made. Score: around 9. Cost: $69. click to buy.

2023 Giacomo Borgogno “No Name” Nebbiolo, Langhe, Piedmont, Italy
Light to medium ruby in color with a hint of orange at the rim, this wine smells of strawberries, molasses, and dried flowers. In the mouth, fleecy tannins coat the mouth and stiffen slightly as flavors of strawberries, orange peel, dried herbs, and dried flowers move across the palate. Excellent bright acidity keeps things fresh, and the tannins remain supple and smooth. 14% alcohol. Comes in an unnecessarily heavy bottle weighing 1.53 kg when full. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $51. click to buy.

2023 Tierra Roja Cabernet Sauvignon, Oakville, Napa, California
Inky dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherries, licorice, and cola. In the mouth, juicy black cherries, cola, licorice, and chocolate-covered espresso beans are all wrapped in fleecy tannins. Excellent acidity keeps the wine from feeling too heavy and ripe, though it is quite rich, with sweet oak lingering in the finish. Barrel-fermented in 75% new French oak and then aged for 20 months. 250 cases made. 14.8% alcohol. Comes in a nasty, heavy bottle weighing 1.63 kg when full. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $215. click to buy.

The post Napa’s Singular Loire Love Affair appeared first on Vinography.
content:
In 1996, after long careers working in Napa’s wine industry, John Skupny and his wife Tracey did something quietly radical: they started a small wine label dedicated exclusively to Cabernet Franc. They named it Lang & Reed, using the two middle names of each of their sons, J Reed Skupny and Jersey Lang Skupny.

These days, especially in California, Cabernet Franc is riding a wave of popularity, with varietal bottlings increasingly common among producers traditionally focused on Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends, as well as with smaller independent producers interested in exploring alternative grape varieties. Demand for the grape has recently hit new highs in Napa, resulting in prices for Cabernet Franc approaching $12,000 per ton, roughly $3,000 higher than the going rate for top-quality Cabernet Sauvignon.

In the late 1990s, however, only a handful of producers in California bottled the grape on its own with any regularity. 

‘Mostly those producers were throwing it in with their Cabernet Sauvignon just so they could say they were making a Bordeaux blend using the right grapes’, says Skupny. ‘If they ever bottled Franc on its own, it was just because they had some left over after their blending.’

To most people in Napa at the time, the idea seemed questionable at best. 

‘Jeff Morgan, who was writing for the Wine Spectator at the time, called me up after I left Inglenook and asked me what I was going to do with myself’, recalls Skupny. ‘I told him that I was going to start a small wine label focused on Cabernet Franc and there was silence on the line for about thirty seconds. I actually thought we might have been disconnected. And then he said, “You’re going to do what?!”’

Napa wasn’t Skupny’s reference point when it came to Cabernet Franc, however. Instead, it was the Loire and Bordeaux’s right bank, where Cabernet Franc plays a starring role.

title: Vinography Unboxed: Week of 8/30/26
summary:
Hello and welcome to my (usually) weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep

The post Vinography Unboxed: Week of 8/30/26 appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Hello and welcome to my (usually) weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This past week included a set of wines from a project called Geographic Wines, which was started by Nuno Morais Vaz and Daniela Matias and, unlike most Portuguese wine companies, it is designed from the start to make wines from a number of different wine regions in Portugal. They make their wines with ambient yeasts, and deliberately pick early to preserve freshness. Vaz and Matias say that they think of themselves as cartographers as much as winemakers, perhaps hence the name. Unfortunately, the project’s website is non-functional so I don’t know the state of the business, but it is clear that these wines are mostly available in Europe at the moment. They are all, both red whites, well made, and most quite good. Keep an eye out for them.

Sticking with Portugal for a moment longer, I also received a sample of a white blend from the Douro made by Quinta Nova de Nossa Senhora do Carmo. That’s a mouthful of a name for a winery (which is why most people just say Quina Nova), and the wine is a tasty mouthful of indigenous white grape varieties grown on the slate soils of the Douro.

Closer to home, Chateau Montelena sent along a bottle of their Riesling from Potter Valley in Mendocino, which does the things you want a Riesling to do in the mouth, though I would love a little bit more acidity than the 2025 vintage yielded.

Las Jaras Wines sent through their “chillable red” wine they call Glou Glou, which is a Carignan- and Zinfandel-driven blend designed to be easy, crunchy, fun, and tasty, and, well, it manages to be all those things.

Finally, we’ll end this week with a couple of venerable old-vine Zinfandels. Aldo’s Vineyard, planted in 1937 is one of the last old-vine vineyards within the city limits of Napa itself, and is surrounded (threatened, actually) on all sides by suburban development. Robert Biale Vineyards has been making wine from the vineyard for a long time, and does a great job of capturing the bright juiciness of the site which contains Abouriou, Valdiguié, Peloursin, St. Peters, Refosco, Mondeuse, and a touch of Pinot Gris in addition to Zinfandel.

The Hayne Vineyard, planted in 1902 near St. Helena in Napa, has been owned by the same family since the 19th Century, and consistently yields fantastic Zinfandel (and a bit of Petite Sirah) fruit for Turley Wine Cellars, who have been bottling it as a single vineyard since at least 1993. It’s dark in complexion but still bright with excellent juiciness.

That’s all for this week. Notes on all these wines below.

Tasting Notes

2021 Geographic Wines “La Volée – Blanc de Noirs Brut Nature” Vinho Espumante Branco, Bairrada, Portugal
Pale gold in the glass with medium-fine bubbles, this wine smells of apple sauce and freshly chopped apples. In the mouth, a faint mousse delivers bright flavors of lemon peel, apples, and a touch of seawater. Dried herbs and a touch of roasted nuts linger in the finish. Excellent acidity and nice clean crispness. 12.5% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $??

2025 Geographic Wines “Landcraft” Alvarinho, Vinho Verde, Portugal
Palest straw-colored in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers, green apple, star fruit, and struck match. In the mouth, salty flavors of green apple, crabapple, lime zest, and wet pavement have a lovely zippy brightness thanks to excellent acidity. 12% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $18. click to buy.

2025 Geographic Wines “Landcraft” Loureiro, Vinho Verde, Portugal
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon peel and grapefruit pith with a hint of white flowers. In the mouth, lemon and pink grapefruit flavors are electric with bright acidity and linger for a long while on the palate. 11.5% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $??

2024 Geographic Wines “Lento” Branco, Douro, Portugal
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of white peach, nectarine, and Asian pears. In the mouth, unripe nectarines, Asian pear, and unripe apple flavors have a bright edge thanks to excellent acidity. Crisp and lean, with a hint of green herbs in the finish. A blend of Rabigato, Viosinho, Gouveio, Códega de Larinho, Síria, and Folgasão. 10.5% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $??

2022 Quinta Nova de Nossa Senhora do Carmo “Grainha Reserva” Branco, Douro, Portugal
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of peaches, white flowers, and pastry cream. In the mouth, nutty flavors of peach, pastry cream, and grapefruit zest have a lingering vanilla top note and a faint bitterness. Very good acidity. A blend of 30% Gouveio, 35% Viosinho, and 35% Rabigato, aged for 7 months in a combination of second-use French and Hungarian oak. 13.5% alcohol. 45,000 bottles made. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $30. click to buy.

2025 Chateau Montelena Riesling, Potter Valley, Mendocino, California
Palest gold to the point of near colorlessness, this wine smells of asian pears, mandarin zest, and white flowers. In the mouth, flavors of mandarin orange peel, Asian pear, and white flowers are clean and bright with decent acidity. A faint chalky texture lingers in the finish. 13.4% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $35. click to buy.

2025 Las Jaras “Glou Glou” Red Blend, Mendocino County, California
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of cherries and boysenberries. In the mouth, black cherry and boysenberry flavors are bright with notes of orange peel and juicy acidity. Faint dried herbal notes linger in the finish with wispy, gauzy tannins. Excellent acidity. A blend of 44% Carignan, 41% Zinfandel, 12% Petite Sirah, and 3% Vermentino. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $26. click to buy.

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Vinhas Velhas Torto” Red Blend, Douro, Portugal
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of plums, dried flowers, citrus peel, and struck match. In the mouth, bright, zingy acidity makes flavors of citrus peel, plum, and plum skin juicy and bright, as notes of pink peppercorns, dried herbs, and oak mix with the fruit. Fine, tight tannins coat the mouth and remain supple, as orange peel brightness lingers in the finish. A field blend of more than 30 different grape varieties planted in 1920. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $??

2023 Turley Wine Cellars “Hayne Vineyard” Zinfandel, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet with purple highlights, this wine smells of cherries, blackberries, and blueberries. In the mouth, blueberries and cherries are shot through with dried herbs and great acidity. Juicy and silky on the tongue, and quite balanced for its alcohol level. Gauzy tannins. Also contains small amounts of Trousseau, Petite Sirah, and Carignane. 15.2% alcohol. Vineyard planted in 1902. 473 cases made. Score: around 9. Cost: $96. click to buy.

2023 Robert Biale Vineyards “Aldo’s Vineyard” Zinfandel, Oak Knoll District, Napa, California
Dark purple in the glass, this wine smells of licorice, blackberries, blueberries, and herbs. In the mouth, blackberry and blueberry fruit flavors mix with licorice, black pepper, and herbs. Great acidity keeps things very fresh in the mouth as faint tannins coat the mouth. There’s a hint of oak in the finish. Very juicy and delicious. 14.8% alcohol. 315 cases made. Vineyard planted in 1937. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $95. click to buy.

title: Hip-Hop Doesn’t Need Wine, But Wine Just Might Need Hip-Hop
summary:
Despite the fading evening light on Lankershim Boulevard, I had to squint a bit in the dim light of the

The post Hip-Hop Doesn’t Need Wine, But Wine Just Might Need Hip-Hop appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Despite the fading evening light on Lankershim Boulevard, I had to squint a bit in the dim light of the club. The wide-open floor was already beginning to fill up with fashionably dressed people as the sounds of hip-hop coursed through the club’s speakers at a relatively subdued volume.

A glance around the room suggested the action was on the periphery, where several individuals stood behind small tables each holding a couple of wine bottles. I grabbed a proffered wine glass from a side table (noting with a somewhat delayed shock that it was a Zalto Universal) and headed for my first taste, walking up to a table staffed by a young woman wearing a hoodie. With a pleasant hello and a smile, Saskia de Rothschild poured me a taste of 1985 Lafite, and that is when I knew I was in for a wine event unlike anything else I had ever experienced.

This was Vin et Hip-Hop Los Angeles, the first US version of a wine event originally held in 2022 at the venerable Château du Clos de Vougeot in Burgundy. The event sprang from a collaboration between vintner Jeremy Seysses of Domaine Dujac, podcaster and educator Jermaine “Wolf of Wine” Stone, and Milena Berman and Loïc Lamy, the duo behind the experiential marketing agency Hautes Côtes. In its first incarnations, it brought hip-hop performers to the heart of Burgundy for a music-festival-meets-wine-tasting event celebrating two expressions of craft that have historically had only the most tenuous of relationships.

The Birth of Vin et Hip-Hop

As a recent Art History graduate working in Los Angeles art galleries, the young California-born Milena Berman jumped at the chance when she received an offer to join an art tourism company based in Burgundy.

“Three weeks later, sight unseen, I moved to Beaune,” she said when I interviewed her in March. It was something of a dream job, creating bespoke tours to art fairs and museums all over Europe for high-level donors to top museums around the world. But like so many things during the Pandemic, it all came crashing to a halt. Berman looked around at her options and decided she might be able to work in wine.

“I reached out to Domaine Dujac, and I said, I’m not sure what I can do at a winery, maybe marketing and sales,” she recalled. “And they were like, ‘Yeah, we don’t do marketing and sales.'”

But the family clearly saw something in the young woman and found her a position on the administrative side of the business, working closely with winemaker Jeremy Seysses, particularly on activities supporting The Roots Fund, something meaningful to her as an American in the midst of the #BlackLivesMatter movement and moment.

As the world opened back up, Berman decided to leave Dujac and launch her own agency, Hautes Côtes, with partner Loïc Lamy, but just before she did, she ended up helping Dujac put on an event that featured podcaster Jermaine Stone. Berman and Stone hit it off and began discussing other potential events they could collaborate on, and they settled on the idea of a post-harvest party.

“I said to Jermaine that I’d make grilled cheese sandwiches and we could find a DJ, and he could do the playlist for the event, and I could ask Jeremy [Seysses] and a few other winemakers to pour a white wine, and so we made a terrible little logo, and made an announcement, and it sold out in minutes,” said Berman. “We were like, ‘Who’s coming to this?'”

Young interns from all over the world staying in Burgundy for their harvest jobs snapped up many of the inexpensive tickets, but some were locals, like Dominique Lafon.

“Dominique said, ‘This is amazing, next year you have to do it at Clos de Vougeot,’ and we were like, ‘Yeah, right,’ and he said, ‘No, I’m serious, I will go with you and tell them they should do this,'” recalls Berman.

Come as You Are

With Lafon’s urging, the Château du Clos de Vougeot agreed, and Vin et Hip Hop was born. When word came through the grapevine that Mike D was coming to Burgundy to be inducted into the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin, the opportunity proved too good to pass up. Introductions were made, and the Beastie Boys founder agreed to DJ the inaugural event following his induction.

From the outset, the organizers envisioned an experience with far more accessibility than the black-tie affairs that have made the Château du Clos de Vougeot legendary among wine lovers.

“We were like, ‘Come in your jeans, come as you are,'” said Berman, “and we wanted the tickets to be less than 100 bucks with dinner included.” The organizers set aside a portion of the proceeds to benefit The Roots Fund.

The resulting event was certainly unlike anything that the Château had ever hosted: 700 young people (and a few older folks, too) partying to the sounds of hip-hop while tasting Burgundies from top producers. In a model that has continued through all subsequent events, producers made bottles available for sale to attendees, who, in the fashion of La Paulée, could open them and share with friends, acquaintances, and strangers throughout the night.

“We talk about how wine can reach different audiences, but sometimes wine needs help,” said Icy Liu, of Becky Wasserman & Co., one of the event’s sponsors. “Wine has had a very different way of relating and representing itself and being engaged with culture in a certain way for a long time, but it’s maybe a bit out of touch with the mainstream of the culture. Hip-hop is cool. The artists are always driving the dialogue with what we’re wearing, where we’re eating, and what we’re doing. Hip-hop is shaping cultural identity.”

That sense of connection with mainstream culture, as well as the passionate communities that have arisen around hip-hop, became a core tenet of the event, which now describes one of its primary goals as “bridging worlds through cultural exchange.”

In addition to the several editions of the event held at Clos de Vougeot, the organizers have also put on Pop et Hip-Hop in the Champagne region. After several years of European events, American wine and hip-hop lovers clamored for a domestic version, and in a lobbying campaign that I imagine was something like the competition for Olympic host cities, Los Angeles won the right to host the first event on American soil.

A Los Angeles Exclusive

The 2026 event in Los Angeles at Verse was unlike any wine event I’ve attended across a number of dimensions. The wines being poured for attendees were spectacular: Vintage Krug Champagne, Billecart-Salmon Elisabeth Salmon Rosé, Domaine de Montille 1er Cru Les Sizies, Dalla Valle Maya, Harlan Estate, Colgin IX Estate, Jaboulet Hermitage La Chapelle, Château Lafleur, Comtes Lafon 1er Cru Meursault-Charmes, Domaine Dujac 1er Cru Aux Combottes, Michel Lafarge Volnay, Domaine Fourrier 1er Cru Combe aux Moines Gevrey-Chambertin, and yes, 1985 Château Lafite Rothschild, among many others.

The crowd was impressively diverse, in both age and race, and the vibe was electric even before the performers took the stage. Common, Keyon Harrold, Dominique Sanders, Jason L. Martin, Dilated Peoples, and a guest appearance from Wiz Khalifa kept the room thumping until late, while the parking lot was filled with food trucks dishing up everything from smash burgers to caviar bumps.

A team of sommeliers behind the bar handled an enthusiastic crowd of spendy wine lovers who were more than happy to deplete the stocks of wines from Burgundy, Champagne, Napa, Bordeaux, Abruzzo, and the Rhône being sold at eye-poppingly excellent prices. Not to unnecessarily tantalize you, but a 2021 Arnoux-Lachaux Vosne-Romanée was on offer that night for $250. Try to find that bottle at retail today, and you’ll pay somewhere north of $600.

The catch to all this was the price of entry. This party and concert (which Hautes Côtes flew me down to LA to attend) had no tickets. Attendance was by invitation only. And to secure an invitation, you had to purchase a seat at one of the many winemaker dinners that preceded the event, with price tags starting at $850 and going up to more than $2,500. I believe the capacity of the club topped out at around 200 people.

Standing there with a $78 hand-blown wine glass filled with $500-per-bottle Burgundy, watching Common freestyle his way through a verse about drinking wine, I didn’t exactly feel part of anything close to “the mainstream.” I was lucky enough to attend an event the likes of which few people have ever had the opportunity to experience. Rarified doesn’t begin to describe it, and that struck me as quite the opposite of what Vin et Hip Hop was trying to achieve, significant donations to The Roots Fund notwithstanding.

When I put this to winemaker Jeremy Seysses and to Berman, they both agreed that the level of exclusivity featured in this event was not in alignment with the mission and vision for Vin et Hip-Hop long term, and reflected more of the specific opportunity they had to partner with the Verse supper club, owned by Grammy-award-winning sound engineer Manny Marroquin.

“I want to see something much bigger in the US,” said Seysses, “closer to or even bigger than what we do at Clos de Vougeot, with similar ticket prices.”

I’d love to see that, too.

A Deserving Synergy

At a time when wine seems to be struggling for relevance with younger generations of drinkers, and demand is shrinking, the appeal of Vin et Hip-Hop becomes obvious. Making inroads with hip-hop’s own diverse audience, and more specifically Black wine drinkers, seems not just smart but imperative. Taking wine off its pedestal and putting it in contexts where it connects with other dimensions of culture offers an opportunity to have different conversations or even just experience wine in different moods. A festival called Blood of Gods, named after a ‘zine of the same name, is doing something similar with heavy metal music in Washington State.

Can events such as these truly change the world of wine, a few hundred people at a time? That remains to be seen. At the very least, they represent something novel and exciting in an industry that seems convinced we’ll all be enthused by a press release touting the latest 90-point scores or the achievement of a new sustainability certification.

Wine needs to be more fun. And it needs to be more fun to a lot more people than it has in the past if the industry is going to survive and thrive. It also needs to connect with communities of passion, and especially those that have at their center things other than wine itself.

Wine also needs to be a bigger, more welcoming place for populations that have historically not been part of the wine conversation, for people who haven’t historically seen many people who look like them engaging with and enjoying wine.

These, I believe, are the glimmers of promise that can be seen amidst the strobes and heard amongst the thumping bass beats of Vin et Hip-Hop. Whether Vin et Hip-Hop can hold onto that promise while retaining its founding ethos (come in your jeans, come as you are) is the harder trick, and the one worth watching (or listening) for.

The next Vin et Hip-Hop event will take place on October 14th, 2026 at the Château du Clos de Vougeot in Burgundy. Tickets went on sale today, September 16th at 5 PM Central European Time, and were sold out almost instantly, as 5300 people attempted to register simultaneously.

The Hatues Côtes team is already working on Vin et Hip Hop for 2027, with events planned in New York and Los Angeles in March, Champagne in June, and another Burgundy event in October. Bordeaux is purportedly in the works too.

Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This week I received a couple of wines from Shared Notes Wines, the Sauvignon Blanc-focused project by the wife-and-husband winemaking team of Bibiana Gonzalez Rave and Jeff Pisoni. I’m reviewing both of the wines they make under that brand this week, and both are excellent, with the caveat that their packaging in big, heavy bottles is effectively a big middle finger to the environment. There’s just no reason to package wines like this in bottles that literally weigh more than the wine they contain. Jeff and Bibiana should know better. OK, off of my soapbox, I think I prefer the straight Sauvignon Blanc to their blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon, at least in the 2025 vintage. I love that both are harvested to result in lean, snappy wines that still have some herbaceous qualities in addition to their sunny fruit. Not everyone will be on board with paying nearly $100 for a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, but those who are will find these wines enjoyable.

Chateau Montelena sent through their Sauvignon Blanc as well, and it seemed rather subdued in comparison to the Shared Notes wines, though it is also half the price.

This week I’m reviewing the Cuvée Esme Ann Chenin Blanc from Las Jaras Wines, which is one of my favorite California Chenins for its reductive, snappy, mouthwatering qualities. The fruit comes from the Junius Vineyard (formerly known as Norgard) in Mendocino County and is barrel-fermented and aged in oak, followed by 9 months in stainless steel.

This week I’m also reviewing another batch of wines from Geographic Wines, a project based in Portugal focused on making wines from many of the country’s different wine regions. This week I enjoyed their white blend from old vines in the Douro as well as their old vine red blend of more than 45 grape varieties from the same place. Sadly, these wines aren’t well distributed outside of Europe, so no buying links to offer to my readers for these. Also, the brand’s website is broken, so I can’t even give you somewhere to learn more about them.

I’ve got a couple of old-vine Zinfandels to recommend this week, from Limerick Lane Cellars, whose Marquis Zinfandel comes from a number of storied old-vine Zinfandel vineyards around Sonoma County and has a tremendous juicy lift with little trace of its substantial alcohol levels.

The 2023 Ridge Lytton Springs is a perennial favorite of mine for its complexity, impressive ageworthiness, and just generally mouthwatering offering of blue and black fruits. The 2023 vintage is an impressive edition of this wine that will likely be great for decades.

Speaking of the 2023 vintage, it also did good things for Tierra Roja wines in Napa’s Oakville AVA, where proprietor Linda Neal farms just over 4 acres of Cabernet Sauvignon. Neal worked as a vineyard manager for others in Napa for many years before deciding to focus exclusively on her own property. She makes just a single wine from the plot each year, and the 2023 vintage is certainly one of the best that winemaker Benoit Touquette has made for her.

The name Giacomo Borgogno is well known in Italy’s Piedmont region for having made Barolo since 1761, making it the oldest continuously operating producer in the region. As in many European countries, Italian wines are subject to tasting panels before they are approved to carry the Barolo DOCG designation. In 2005, Borgogno submitted two cask samples to the tasting commission, and one was rejected for not seeming typical in color, despite being made exactly the same as the one that had been accepted. In protest, Borgogno declassified the wine, and No Name Langhe Nebbiolo was born, bearing the designation “a protest label” against appellation bureaucracy. Since then, the Borgogno family has continued to deliberately declassify a portion of their Barolo production each year to make the wine. It is always excellent.

Notes on all these below.

Tasting Notes

2025 Shared Notes “Les Leçons des Maîtres” White Blend, Russian River Valley, Sonoma, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass—nearly colorless—this wine smells of passionfruit, green bell peppers, and honeysuckle. In the mouth, silky, salty flavors of chopped green herbs, green apple skin, and gooseberries have a nice brightness thanks to excellent acidity. A blend of 75% Sauvignon Blanc and 25% Semillon. 13.5% alcohol. 266 cases made. Comes in an unnecessarily heavy bottle weighing 1.54 kg when full. Score: around 9. Cost: $95. click to buy.

2025 Shared Notes “Les Pierres Qui Décident” Sauvignon Blanc, North Coast, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of green apple, passionfruit, cut grass, and a hint of green bell peppers. In the mouth, candied green apple, passionfruit, and gooseberry flavors are electrically bright with excellent acidity and shot through with a hint of crushed nuts and alfalfa. Bright and juicy. A blend of fruit from Sonoma County (70%) and Napa County (30%). 12.87% alcohol. Comes in a nasty, heavy bottle weighing 1.63 kg when full. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $95. click to buy.

2025 Chateau Montelena Sauvignon Blanc, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Palest greenish gold in color, this wine smells of lime zest, green apples, and white flowers. In the mouth, green apple and kiwi notes have a faint grassy quality to them, as well as decent acidity. 14.2% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2023 Las Jaras “Cuvée Esme Anne” Chenin Blanc, Mendocino County, California
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of struck match, Asian pear, honeysuckle, and candied ginger. In the mouth, candied ginger, Asian pear, struck match, and wet pavement flavors are saline and bright with juicy acidity. Lean and bright, with lovely persistence. Barrel-fermented and aged in oak, followed by 9 months in stainless steel. Bottled unfiltered. 13% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $68.

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Vinhas Velhas Chão de Areia” Vinho Branco, Douro, Portugal
Pale yellow-gold in color, this wine smells of yellow plum, nectarine, and struck flint. In the mouth, salty flavors of unripe nectarines, pomelo zest, saffron, and dried herbs are bright and juicy with a hint of oaky nuttiness. Excellent acidity. A field blend of Rabigato, Viosinho, Gouveio, Códega de Larinho, Síria, and Folgasão. 12% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: ??

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Canais” Touriga Nacional, Douro, Portugal
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black tea, black cherries, crushed peppercorns, and dried herbs. In the mouth, fleecy tannins wrap around a core of black cherries, black tea, and dried herbs. Very good acidity. The tannins gain weight and stiffness with time. 12.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $??

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Vinhas Velhas Almendra” Red Blend, Douro, Portugal
Medium to dark garnet in color, this wine smells of black cherries, black plum, bergamot, earth, and dried flowers. In the mouth, smooth, suede-like tannins coat the mouth and surround a core of black cherries, black plum, currants, dried herbs, and wildflowers. Excellent acidity, lovely balance, and poise. Comes from a field blend of more than 45 different varieties planted in 1850. 12.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $??

2023 Ridge Vineyards “Lytton Springs” Red Blend, Dry Creek Valley, Sonoma, California
Dark purple in the glass, this wine smells of blackberries, black pepper, boysenberries, and cocoa powder. In the mouth, blackberry pie and cocoa powder flavors are wrapped in powdery, mouth-coating tannins that linger with licorice, dried herbs, and sandalwood in the finish. Excellent acidity and balance. 14.4% alcohol. A blend of 76% Zinfandel, 14% Petite Sirah, 7% Carignan, 2% Alicante Bouschet, and 1% Mataro. Vineyard planted in 1905. 11,800 cases made. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $56. click to buy.

2023 Limerick Lane Cellars “Marquis” Zinfandel, Russian River Valley, Sonoma, California
Very dark garnet in color, this wine smells of blackberries, licorice, and flowers. In the mouth, juicy floral flavors of boysenberries, raspberries, and orange peel are wrapped in supple, athletic tannins. Great acidity. 15.1% alcohol. 350 cases made. Score: around 9. Cost: $69. click to buy.

2023 Giacomo Borgogno “No Name” Nebbiolo, Langhe, Piedmont, Italy
Light to medium ruby in color with a hint of orange at the rim, this wine smells of strawberries, molasses, and dried flowers. In the mouth, fleecy tannins coat the mouth and stiffen slightly as flavors of strawberries, orange peel, dried herbs, and dried flowers move across the palate. Excellent bright acidity keeps things fresh, and the tannins remain supple and smooth. 14% alcohol. Comes in an unnecessarily heavy bottle weighing 1.53 kg when full. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $51. click to buy.

2023 Tierra Roja Cabernet Sauvignon, Oakville, Napa, California
Inky dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherries, licorice, and cola. In the mouth, juicy black cherries, cola, licorice, and chocolate-covered espresso beans are all wrapped in fleecy tannins. Excellent acidity keeps the wine from feeling too heavy and ripe, though it is quite rich, with sweet oak lingering in the finish. Barrel-fermented in 75% new French oak and then aged for 20 months. 250 cases made. 14.8% alcohol. Comes in a nasty, heavy bottle weighing 1.63 kg when full. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $215. click to buy.

title: Napa’s Singular Loire Love Affair
summary:
In 1996, after long careers working in Napa’s wine industry, John Skupny and his wife Tracey did something quietly radical:

The post Napa’s Singular Loire Love Affair appeared first on Vinography.
content:
In 1996, after long careers working in Napa’s wine industry, John Skupny and his wife Tracey did something quietly radical: they started a small wine label dedicated exclusively to Cabernet Franc. They named it Lang & Reed, using the two middle names of each of their sons, J Reed Skupny and Jersey Lang Skupny.

These days, especially in California, Cabernet Franc is riding a wave of popularity, with varietal bottlings increasingly common among producers traditionally focused on Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends, as well as with smaller independent producers interested in exploring alternative grape varieties. Demand for the grape has recently hit new highs in Napa, resulting in prices for Cabernet Franc approaching $12,000 per ton, roughly $3,000 higher than the going rate for top-quality Cabernet Sauvignon.

In the late 1990s, however, only a handful of producers in California bottled the grape on its own with any regularity. 

‘Mostly those producers were throwing it in with their Cabernet Sauvignon just so they could say they were making a Bordeaux blend using the right grapes’, says Skupny. ‘If they ever bottled Franc on its own, it was just because they had some left over after their blending.’

To most people in Napa at the time, the idea seemed questionable at best. 

‘Jeff Morgan, who was writing for the Wine Spectator at the time, called me up after I left Inglenook and asked me what I was going to do with myself’, recalls Skupny. ‘I told him that I was going to start a small wine label focused on Cabernet Franc and there was silence on the line for about thirty seconds. I actually thought we might have been disconnected. And then he said, “You’re going to do what?!”’

Napa wasn’t Skupny’s reference point when it came to Cabernet Franc, however. Instead, it was the Loire and Bordeaux’s right bank, where Cabernet Franc plays a starring role.

summary:
Hello and welcome to my (usually) weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep

content:
Hello and welcome to my (usually) weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This past week included a set of wines from a project called Geographic Wines, which was started by Nuno Morais Vaz and Daniela Matias and, unlike most Portuguese wine companies, it is designed from the start to make wines from a number of different wine regions in Portugal. They make their wines with ambient yeasts, and deliberately pick early to preserve freshness. Vaz and Matias say that they think of themselves as cartographers as much as winemakers, perhaps hence the name. Unfortunately, the project’s website is non-functional so I don’t know the state of the business, but it is clear that these wines are mostly available in Europe at the moment. They are all, both red whites, well made, and most quite good. Keep an eye out for them.

Sticking with Portugal for a moment longer, I also received a sample of a white blend from the Douro made by Quinta Nova de Nossa Senhora do Carmo. That’s a mouthful of a name for a winery (which is why most people just say Quina Nova), and the wine is a tasty mouthful of indigenous white grape varieties grown on the slate soils of the Douro.

Closer to home, Chateau Montelena sent along a bottle of their Riesling from Potter Valley in Mendocino, which does the things you want a Riesling to do in the mouth, though I would love a little bit more acidity than the 2025 vintage yielded.

Las Jaras Wines sent through their “chillable red” wine they call Glou Glou, which is a Carignan- and Zinfandel-driven blend designed to be easy, crunchy, fun, and tasty, and, well, it manages to be all those things.

Finally, we’ll end this week with a couple of venerable old-vine Zinfandels. Aldo’s Vineyard, planted in 1937 is one of the last old-vine vineyards within the city limits of Napa itself, and is surrounded (threatened, actually) on all sides by suburban development. Robert Biale Vineyards has been making wine from the vineyard for a long time, and does a great job of capturing the bright juiciness of the site which contains Abouriou, Valdiguié, Peloursin, St. Peters, Refosco, Mondeuse, and a touch of Pinot Gris in addition to Zinfandel.

The Hayne Vineyard, planted in 1902 near St. Helena in Napa, has been owned by the same family since the 19th Century, and consistently yields fantastic Zinfandel (and a bit of Petite Sirah) fruit for Turley Wine Cellars, who have been bottling it as a single vineyard since at least 1993. It’s dark in complexion but still bright with excellent juiciness.

That’s all for this week. Notes on all these wines below.

Tasting Notes

2021 Geographic Wines “La Volée – Blanc de Noirs Brut Nature” Vinho Espumante Branco, Bairrada, Portugal
Pale gold in the glass with medium-fine bubbles, this wine smells of apple sauce and freshly chopped apples. In the mouth, a faint mousse delivers bright flavors of lemon peel, apples, and a touch of seawater. Dried herbs and a touch of roasted nuts linger in the finish. Excellent acidity and nice clean crispness. 12.5% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $??

2025 Geographic Wines “Landcraft” Alvarinho, Vinho Verde, Portugal
Palest straw-colored in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers, green apple, star fruit, and struck match. In the mouth, salty flavors of green apple, crabapple, lime zest, and wet pavement have a lovely zippy brightness thanks to excellent acidity. 12% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $18. click to buy.

2025 Geographic Wines “Landcraft” Loureiro, Vinho Verde, Portugal
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon peel and grapefruit pith with a hint of white flowers. In the mouth, lemon and pink grapefruit flavors are electric with bright acidity and linger for a long while on the palate. 11.5% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $??

2024 Geographic Wines “Lento” Branco, Douro, Portugal
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of white peach, nectarine, and Asian pears. In the mouth, unripe nectarines, Asian pear, and unripe apple flavors have a bright edge thanks to excellent acidity. Crisp and lean, with a hint of green herbs in the finish. A blend of Rabigato, Viosinho, Gouveio, Códega de Larinho, Síria, and Folgasão. 10.5% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $??

2022 Quinta Nova de Nossa Senhora do Carmo “Grainha Reserva” Branco, Douro, Portugal
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of peaches, white flowers, and pastry cream. In the mouth, nutty flavors of peach, pastry cream, and grapefruit zest have a lingering vanilla top note and a faint bitterness. Very good acidity. A blend of 30% Gouveio, 35% Viosinho, and 35% Rabigato, aged for 7 months in a combination of second-use French and Hungarian oak. 13.5% alcohol. 45,000 bottles made. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $30. click to buy.

2025 Chateau Montelena Riesling, Potter Valley, Mendocino, California
Palest gold to the point of near colorlessness, this wine smells of asian pears, mandarin zest, and white flowers. In the mouth, flavors of mandarin orange peel, Asian pear, and white flowers are clean and bright with decent acidity. A faint chalky texture lingers in the finish. 13.4% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $35. click to buy.

2025 Las Jaras “Glou Glou” Red Blend, Mendocino County, California
Light garnet in the glass, this wine smells of cherries and boysenberries. In the mouth, black cherry and boysenberry flavors are bright with notes of orange peel and juicy acidity. Faint dried herbal notes linger in the finish with wispy, gauzy tannins. Excellent acidity. A blend of 44% Carignan, 41% Zinfandel, 12% Petite Sirah, and 3% Vermentino. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $26. click to buy.

2023 Geographic Wines “Inóspito – Vinhas Velhas Torto” Red Blend, Douro, Portugal
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of plums, dried flowers, citrus peel, and struck match. In the mouth, bright, zingy acidity makes flavors of citrus peel, plum, and plum skin juicy and bright, as notes of pink peppercorns, dried herbs, and oak mix with the fruit. Fine, tight tannins coat the mouth and remain supple, as orange peel brightness lingers in the finish. A field blend of more than 30 different grape varieties planted in 1920. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $??

2023 Turley Wine Cellars “Hayne Vineyard” Zinfandel, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet with purple highlights, this wine smells of cherries, blackberries, and blueberries. In the mouth, blueberries and cherries are shot through with dried herbs and great acidity. Juicy and silky on the tongue, and quite balanced for its alcohol level. Gauzy tannins. Also contains small amounts of Trousseau, Petite Sirah, and Carignane. 15.2% alcohol. Vineyard planted in 1902. 473 cases made. Score: around 9. Cost: $96. click to buy.

2023 Robert Biale Vineyards “Aldo’s Vineyard” Zinfandel, Oak Knoll District, Napa, California
Dark purple in the glass, this wine smells of licorice, blackberries, blueberries, and herbs. In the mouth, blackberry and blueberry fruit flavors mix with licorice, black pepper, and herbs. Great acidity keeps things very fresh in the mouth as faint tannins coat the mouth. There’s a hint of oak in the finish. Very juicy and delicious. 14.8% alcohol. 315 cases made. Vineyard planted in 1937. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $95. click to buy.
